title: Taiwan Non-Discrimination Act of 2025
official_title: To require the Secretary of the Treasury to pursue more equitable treatment of Taiwan at the international financial institutions, and for other purposes.
summary: The Taiwan Non-Discrimination Act requires the U.S. representative at the International Monetary Fund to advocate for Taiwan's admission as a member of the IMF, its participation in IMF economic surveillance, employment opportunities for Taiwan nationals at the IMF, and Taiwan's access to IMF technical assistance and training. The requirement sunsets when Taiwan is admitted or after 10 years.
brief: Directs the U.S. IMF representative to actively support Taiwan's IMF membership, surveillance participation, employment access, and technical assistance, and requires the Secretary of the Treasury to address Taiwan participation in each of the next 7 years the Secretary is required to present testimony under section 1705(b) of the International Financial Institutions Act.

top_lines.headline: U.S. Must Advocate for Taiwan at IMF
subs: U.S. Governor of the IMF must use voice and vote to support Taiwan's admission as a member, if Taiwan seeks admission
Must also support Taiwan's participation in IMF surveillance activities, employment of Taiwan nationals, and Taiwan's access to technical assistance
Secretary of the Treasury may waive requirements for up to 1 year at a time if providing the waiver promotes Taiwan's meaningful participation at international financial institutions

top_lines.headline: Reporting and Sunset
subs: Secretary of the Treasury must include Taiwan participation efforts in the next 7 years the Secretary is required to present testimony under section 1705(b) of the International Financial Institutions Act
Section 4 requirements expire when Taiwan is admitted to the IMF or after 10 years, whichever is earlier

likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House and has been placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar, suggesting some momentum. However, with only 3 cosponsors in the House, it has limited visible support. Taiwan's IMF membership is complicated by China's opposition, and some senators may be reluctant to direct Treasury votes at the IMF on such a sensitive diplomatic issue. A Senate floor vote has not been scheduled.

items.main: Names the Act the “Taiwan Non-Discrimination Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: States congressional findings on Taiwan's economy and its standing at international financial institutions, including that Taiwan is the 21st largest economy and 10th largest U.S. goods trading partner and held $471.9B in foreign exchange reserves (Jan. 2020 Treasury report).
items.detail: Findings section — recites background (IMF Articles of Agreement, the Taiwan Relations Act (Public Law 96-8) sec. 4(d), Taiwan's prior 1980 IMF membership, Kosovo's IMF/World Bank membership); no operative effect.

items.main: Expresses the sense of Congress that the size and connectedness of Taiwan's economy highlight the importance of greater Taiwan participation in the IMF, and that Taiwan's democratic, rule-of-law economic development should inform the work of the international financial institutions.
items.detail: Sense-of-Congress statement — no substantive legal effect.

sections.label: Section 4 — Support for Taiwan Admission to the IMF

items.main: Requires the U.S. Governor of the IMF to use the U.S. voice and vote to support Taiwan's admission as a member, Taiwan's participation in Article IV surveillance consultations, employment of Taiwan nationals at the IMF without nationality-based restrictions, and Taiwan's access to IMF technical assistance.
items.detail: Taiwan held IMF membership until China was seated in 1980. The bill notes that Taiwan is the 21st largest economy in the world and the 10th largest U.S. goods trading partner, and cites IMF Articles allowing membership by 'countries' without requiring statehood as a condition. The Secretary of the Treasury may waive any requirement of this section for up to one year by reporting to Congress that the waiver will substantially promote the objective of securing Taiwan's meaningful participation at international financial institutions. The section expires when Taiwan is admitted or after 10 years.

items.main: Requires that in each of the next 7 years in which the Secretary of the Treasury is required by section 1705(b) of the International Financial Institutions Act to present testimony, the Secretary include a description of U.S. efforts to support the greatest practicable Taiwan participation at each international financial institution.
items.detail: “International financial institution” defined by reference to section 1701(c)(2) of the International Financial Institutions Act.

gaps: The bill requires the U.S. IMF Governor to support Taiwan's admission but does not require the U.S. to vote against any IMF action that would further marginalize Taiwan, such as surveillance exclusions or staffing restrictions.

The bill is conditioned on Taiwan seeking admission; if Taiwan chooses not to formally apply, the core admission advocacy requirement in Section 4(a)(1) does not activate, even though the bill's findings indicate Taiwan announced it would seek membership in October 2024.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Sherman
featured_quotes.text: H.R. 910 is a bipartisan bill that requires that the United States use its vote and its voice at the IMF to support Taiwan's membership. Taiwan has been an excellent contributor to the global economy and should not be absent from organizations such as the IMF. Congress should support this bill, and I urge my Republican colleagues not only to urge that Donald Trump carry this bill out but also support the people of Taiwan and support the role of the IMF as we go forward.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Kim
featured_quotes.text: I would also like to thank Representative Green of Texas for co-leading H.R. 910 and making this a bipartisan effort. This bill is simple. It requires the Treasury Department to advocate for Taiwan to join the International Monetary Fund, or IMF. Unfortunately, China has consistently blocked Taiwan's participation in international forums, including IMF. China pursues these tactics because they know that financial security is just as important as military security.

added: Statutory requirement for U.S. IMF Governor to advocate for Taiwan's IMF admission, surveillance participation, employment access, and technical assistance
Requirement that Taiwan participation efforts be included in the next 7 years of Treasury testimony under section 1705(b) of the International Financial Institutions Act
U.S. policy declaration not to discourage or deter Taiwan from seeking IMF membership
Statutory citation "(22 U.S.C. 262r(c)(2))" added after the two references to section 1701(c)(2) of the International Financial Institutions Act (Secs. 4(c) and 5)
